strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap at the intersection of continual learning and cooperative MARL, with clear motivation and real-world analogies (AVs, warehouse robots).

The JAX-based, end-to-end GPU-accelerated pipeline is a valuable engineering contribution, enabling task sequences (up to 100 tasks) far longer than prior CPU-bound CL benchmarks (5-15 tasks), which should meaningfully lower the barrier to entry for CMARL research.

The procedural generation pipeline with a formal solvability validator (Appendix A.2-A.3) is well engineered and provides an effectively unbounded, reproducible (seed-controlled) task distribution rather than a fixed static set, addressing overfitting concerns raised by prior Overcooked robustness work.

Breadth of empirical investigation is impressive: six CL baselines across three difficulty levels, an architectural ablation (multi-head, task-ID, CNN vs MLP, critic regularization, layer norm), N-agent scaling (1-3 agents), network plasticity analysis via repetition, reward-design comparisons (shared/individual/sparse), partial observability, curriculum learning, and heterogeneous role assignment.

Principled normalization scheme (single-agent optimal cook-deliver cycle) allows comparison of normalized scores across heterogeneously sized/structured procedurally generated layouts, and continual learning metrics (average score, forgetting, forward transfer) are formally defined and computed with confidence intervals.
Extensive appendix detailing hyperparameters, network architecture, generator/validator pseudocode, and additional per-task curves supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The benchmark is built entirely on a single domain (Overcooked) with a single underlying MARL backbone (IPPO) for almost all main results; MAPPO and QMIX/VDN-style value-decomposition methods, which are standard in cooperative MARL, are only briefly touched (Section 5.7) rather than integrated as first-class baselines, limiting how representative the findings are for CMARL broadly despite the paper's benchmark framing.

Only the task-incremental setting (oracle task identity supplied at train and test time) is studied; this is an easier and less realistic CL protocol than task-agnostic/class-incremental settings, and the paper does not empirically probe how methods behave without this oracle signal, despite acknowledging it as a limitation.

Difficulty levels are defined by coarse heuristics (grid size ranges and obstacle density percentages) rather than a validated or continuous difficulty measure; the mapping from these surface statistics to 'coordination difficulty' is asserted rather than empirically justified (e.g., no correlation analysis between the chosen knobs and achieved task difficulty).

Many of the additional studies (curriculum learning, heterogeneous roles, reward design, N-agent) are single-setting demonstrations with only one sequence configuration and comparatively small sample sizes/high variance (e.g., Table 8 shows overlapping confidence intervals for the medium-difficulty comparison), so several conclusions are more suggestive than rigorously established.

Explanations for some counterintuitive findings (e.g., MAPPO underperforming IPPO under continual learning, Section 5.7) remain speculative ('a plausible cause...') without additional diagnostic experiments (e.g., analyzing critic value drift directly) to substantiate the proposed mechanism.

The normalized score's single-agent optimal-cycle upper bound is a heuristic approximation (ignoring two-agent parallelization) that can allow scores 'above 1'; while acknowledged, this makes cross-layout and cross-method comparisons somewhat approximate rather than exact, and the bound's tightness/looseness is not empirically validated against, e.g., a brute-force multi-agent optimum on small layouts.

The paper reports 5 seeds throughout; while confidence intervals are shown, some comparisons (e.g., EWC vs Online EWC on Level 2 in Table 11, CI ±0.34) have very wide intervals that undercut the strength of claims drawn from point-estimate rankings in the main text discussion.

As a resource/benchmark paper, the actual methodological contribution is limited to reimplementing six existing single-agent CL methods in JAX combined with IPPO; no new CMARL-specific algorithm is proposed, so the paper's value rests almost entirely on the benchmark's future adoption, which cannot be assessed at submission time.

strengths: Addresses a clear and underexplored gap at the intersection of continual learning and cooperative MARL, for which no dedicated benchmark previously existed.

The JAX-based, end-to-end GPU-accelerated implementation is a genuine engineering contribution: it enables training on sequences of up to 100 tasks in a few hours on a single desktop GPU, a large improvement in throughput over CPU-bound CL/MARL benchmarks (CORA, Continual World, COOM).

Procedural level generator with an explicit solvability validator (10 reachability/usability checks) provides a virtually unlimited, reproducible, and seed-controlled supply of tasks, mitigating overfitting to a fixed set of layouts.

Reasonably comprehensive evaluation protocol: three complementary metrics (Average Performance, Forgetting, Plasticity), multiple CL baselines (FT, L2, EWC, Online EWC, MAS) combined with IPPO, and an ablation study isolating architectural factors (multi-head outputs, task ID, critic regularization, layer norm, CNN vs MLP).
The plasticity-loss experiment (repeating a task sequence multiple times) is a nice additional analysis connecting the CMARL setting to known single-agent continual RL pathologies.
Good documentation of implementation details in the appendix (generator algorithm, validator logic, upper-bound soup estimator, hyperparameters), which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The abstract and conclusion state that methods are shown to 'fail to scale to more complex settings' and that 'parameter-isolation methods fail to scale with longer task sequences,' but no parameter-isolation method (e.g., PackNet, mentioned in Related Work) is actually evaluated in the experiments; only regularization-based methods and naive fine-tuning are tested, creating a mismatch between claims and evidence.

The bulk of the detailed analysis (Figures 3-6, Table 2-3) is conducted only on Level 1 (easy) 20-task or 10-task sequences; Level 2 and Level 3 results are confined to a single appendix figure (Figure 7) with EWC only, so the central claim about performance degradation on harder settings is comparatively under-supported.

The domain remains narrow: all environments are variants of a single two-agent, fully-observable, discrete-action Overcooked-style kitchen. Despite the procedural generator, this limits the generality of conclusions about CMARL more broadly (e.g., no partial observability, no larger agent counts, no competitive or mixed-motive settings), a point the authors do acknowledge in Limitations.

Only one MARL backbone (IPPO) is evaluated, despite the Related Work section discussing VDN, QMIX, and MAPPO as alternative and potentially more coordination-aware algorithms; it is unclear whether the observed failure modes are specific to IPPO or general to MARL+CL combinations.

The task-incremental setting (task ID available during training) is the only continual learning paradigm studied, which is a relatively easy CL regime; more challenging class- or domain-incremental analogues for MARL are left entirely to future work.

The normalized scoring metric relies on a single-agent optimal cook-deliver cycle heuristic, which by the authors' own admission underestimates true throughput when multi-agent parallelization is possible, introducing potential noise/bias into cross-layout comparisons that is not empirically quantified.

No human-in-the-loop or zero-shot coordination evaluation is included despite the introduction motivating the work partly via human-AI coordination and autonomous vehicle scenarios, making the applied motivation somewhat disconnected from the actual experiments.
